objectives.text: Establish the first government-wide AML/CFT national priorities to assist covered institutions in meeting their obligations under AML/CFT laws and regulations.

citations.quote:
is issuing these first government-
wide priorities for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/
CFT) policy (the “Priorities”).

The establishment of these Priorities is intended 
to assist all covered institutions 6 in their efforts to meet their obligations under laws and 
regulations designed to combat money laundering and counter terrorist financing.

objectives.text: Identify eight AML/CFT priorities (in no particular order): corruption; cybercrime; foreign and domestic terrorist financing; fraud; transnational criminal organization activity; drug trafficking organization activity; human trafficking and human smuggling; and proliferation financing.

citations.quote:
the Priorities are, in no particular order: (1) corruption; 
(2) cybercrime, including relevant cybersecurity and virtual currency considerations; (3) 
foreign and domestic terrorist financing; (4) fraud; (5) transnational criminal organization 
activity; (6) drug trafficking organization activity; (7) human trafficking and human 
smuggling; and (8) proliferation financing.

obligations.action: issue regulations that will specify how financial institutions should incorporate these Priorities into their risk-based AML programs

citations.quote:
FinCEN will issue regulations at a later date that will specify how financial institutions 
should incorporate these Priorities into their risk-based AML programs.

obligations.action: review and incorporate, as appropriate, each Priority based on the institution’s broader risk-based AML program
obligations.trigger: upon the effective date of future regulations to be promulgated in connection with these Priorities
exceptions: FinCEN recognizes that not every Priority will be relevant to every covered institution

obligations.action: update the Priorities at least once every four years, as required by the AML Act, to account for new and emerging threats

citations.quote:

notes: This source is FinCEN agency guidance (evidence role: agency_guidance), issued June 30, 2021, with no update as of July 2026 despite the AML Act's four-year update requirement (the pinned-date scope notes the priorities are >4 years old but unrefreshed — preserved as written, not reconciled). The document is largely narrative/descriptive (typologies, threat descriptions) rather than obligation-imposing; most operative duties are hortatory ('should') and expressly deferred to future regulations that 'will specify how financial institutions should incorporate these Priorities.' The 'must comply with sanctions programs' statements reference OFAC/sanctions, which are boundary regimes under the ratified scope; extracted as written because they appear as duties on covered institutions within the program-establishment context (risk-based AML programs), but flagged as boundary-adjacent. SAR filing references (31 CFR x.320) are coordination-layer per scope and recorded only as interactions, not as new obligations. The eight Priorities themselves are descriptive threat categories, not element-table duties, so are captured as objectives. Definitions in footnotes are given verbatim as the source presents them (some are cross-quotations of other statutes/assessments).
